newsitem.title: GERMANY: German call money ticks higher before month-end.
newsitem.headline: German call money ticks higher before month-end.

text.p: German call money rates traded higher on Wednesday as dealers were preparing for month-end which is still expected to pass quite smoothly.
After hovering around the three percent level for a number of days, overnight funds traded between 3.00/3.05 percent today and were expected to nudge even higher on Thursday.
"The short-term trend is for rates to climb a little bit," said a senior Frankfurt-based dealer, referring mostly to month-end conditions.
The Bundesbank this morning added a net 1.5 billion marks in in funds to the system, matching market expectations.
"The Bundesbank gave us exactly what we needed, and things should be pretty smooth even at month-end," another dealer added. Rates could climb to 3.25/50 percent on Thursday.
Overnight comments from a senior Bundesbank council member to a German newspaper however have not yet filtered through to the market.

Hans-Juergen Koebnick, a council member and president of the state central bank in the Rhineland-Palatinate and Saar regions, told German daily Handelsblatt that the Bundesbank would have to act very cautiously while faced with the dilemma of a soft mark and fragile economy.

Koebnick also said the Bundesbank would uphold its stability oriented mandate if import prices continued to rise. The softer mark has impacted on import prices even though this has not yet been translated into a higher cost of living rate.
The inflation-conscious Bundesbank has in the past taken early action to prevent prices from rising too quickly.
Economists have however argued the Bundesbank might shy away from nudging short-term interest rates higher as this would not underpin the mark and would instead strangle economic recovery.

Money market dealers also said Koebnick's comments should not be over-interpreted even though they surely reflected the Bundesbank's prevailing opinion. "He only held a candle into the hole, but we should not begin panicking about this at this moment," a dealer said.

Some traders said the Bundesbank might consider offering both a fixed rate tender as well as a variable rate tender allowing banks to chose how the obtain their funds. The Bundesbank has offered only fixed rate tenders for over a year.
Banks held 41.3 billion marks in reserve at the central bank on Tuesday after 41.0 billion marks on Monday.
The average rate remained at 41.1 billion marks while Lombard borrowings were negligible.
The Frankfurt Interbank Overnight Average FIONA= was set at 3.08067 percent on Wednesday after 3.01667 percent on Tuesday.
